subsection: 7. The changing economy and society: agriculture, industrialisation, urban growth and education

notes.h: What 'Industrial Revolution' means and why Britain went first
notes.b: Between 1815 and 1871 Europe was changing from a world of farmers and craft workers to one of factories and towns. Britain led the way, so it helps to know what the change was and why it began there.
points: Industrialisation, often called the 'Industrial Revolution', was the shift from hand production at home or in small workshops (the domestic system, where families worked for merchants in their own houses) to machine production in factories powered first by water and then by steam.
The British industrial revolution began in the later eighteenth century in cotton textiles, coal and iron, which is why Britain is described as the first industrial nation.
Britain industrialised first because it had coal and iron ore close together, capital (money to invest) from trade and farming, and overseas and colonial markets to sell to.
It also had a large merchant fleet and navy, rivers, canals and ports for moving goods, and political stability, so investors could trust that their factories would not be seized or wrecked by war.
Britain's population roughly doubled between 1801 and 1851 (the first census was in 1801). This gave industry both workers to hire and customers to buy its goods.
A growing population was fed because farming had improved, which is why changes in agriculture and industry belong together in this topic.
Before 1815 most Europeans lived on the land and worked in farming. Western Europe was ahead of central and eastern Europe in both farming and industry, so change was uneven across the continent.
notes.tip: A high-scoring answer on change explains why it happened and how fast in each country, not just a list of inventions. Start from these causes.

notes.h: Enclosure and its effects in Britain
notes.b: Britain's farming was transformed from the eighteenth century onwards. The first big change was in how land was held, because farmers could not improve land that was shared and scattered.
points: Enclosure replaced open fields and common land with compact, hedged farms. In the open-field system villagers farmed scattered strips and shared common land, which made it hard for anyone to try new methods.
Most enclosure was done by private Acts of Parliament. There were thousands of them, and most were passed between 1750 and 1850.
The General Enclosure Acts of 1801 and 1845 simplified the procedure, so landowners no longer needed a separate Act for every village.
The result was larger, more efficient farms and higher output, because owners could drain land, choose crops and breed animals without interference from neighbours.
The cost fell on the poor. Cottagers and labourers (people with a cottage and a few rights on the common but little or no land) lost their common rights and their access to land.
Without land of their own, many became wage labourers, moved to the towns or emigrated, which fed the growth of the industrial towns.
notes.tip: Do not mix up enclosure (consolidating land into farms) with the Corn Laws (tariffs on imported grain). Higher essays on harsh lives for farm workers expect enclosure and the loss of common rights.

notes.h: New crops, rotation and the early improvers
notes.b: Enclosed farms could be run more intelligently. New crop rotations and better breeding allowed farmers to feed more people and more animals from the same land.
points: The Norfolk four-course rotation grew wheat, turnips, barley and clover in turn. It ended the fallow year (a year when land was left unplanted to recover), so every field produced something every year.
Turnips and clover fed livestock through the winter, so farmers could keep more animals and did not have to slaughter many in autumn. More animals also meant more manure to fertilise the fields.
The rotation was popularised in the eighteenth century, and Charles 'Turnip' Townshend is associated with it.
As background from before 1815, Jethro Tull's seed drill (early 1700s) sowed seed in rows at a regular depth, reducing the waste of scattering seed by hand.
Also as background, Robert Bakewell in Leicestershire used selective breeding (choosing the best animals as parents) to improve sheep and cattle, breeding them for meat.
notes.tip: Be specific. A rotation and its reasons (no fallow, winter feed, more manure) earns more than the bare word 'new crops'.

notes.h: Fertilisers, science and machinery on the land
notes.b: From the 1840s science and machines began to raise yields and cut the labour needed on farms. This helped output, but it also left farm workers more insecure.
points: Guano (dried seabird droppings, rich in nutrients) was imported from Peru as fertiliser from the 1840s, so farmers could restore soil without leaving it fallow.
John Bennet Lawes patented superphosphate fertiliser in 1842 and founded the Rothamsted experiments in Hertfordshire, which tested crops and fertilisers scientifically.
Justus von Liebig's book on chemistry applied to agriculture (1840) showed that plants take nutrients from the soil, and field drainage of wet land also raised yields from the 1840s.
The threshing machine, which separates grain from straw, reduced the need for hand labour at harvest. Reapers followed, such as the American McCormick reaper shown at the Great Exhibition in 1851.
Steam power came onto farms later in the period, so machines could do work once done by hand.
Anger over threshing machines, which took away winter work, fed the Swing Riots of 1830 in southern and eastern England, when farm labourers broke the machines.
Life for agricultural workers was harsh: low wages, insecure seasonal work, the loss of common rights and poor cottages. Exams ask about both farm and factory workers.
notes.tip: For a Higher essay on why life was harsh, farm workers need their own evidence: enclosure, lost common rights, mechanisation and the Swing Riots, then the 1840s hunger and emigration.

notes.h: The Corn Laws
notes.b: Grain was Britain's most important crop, and landowners wanted its price kept high. The Corn Laws were their protection.
points: The Corn Law of 1815 banned imports of foreign wheat until the home price was high. This protected British grain growers by keeping out cheap foreign grain.
The same law kept bread dear for townspeople and factory workers, which is why it became a target of free-trade critics.
The Corn Laws were repealed in 1846.
notes.tip: Keep the Corn Laws separate from enclosure in your answers: one is about tariffs on imports, the other about how land was farmed.

notes.h: Agriculture in France and the Prussian lands
notes.b: Farming on the continent changed more slowly than in Britain, and the pattern of landholding depended on what each state had done to the old system of lords and peasants.
points: In France the Revolution of 1789 abolished feudal dues (payments peasants owed to their lords). By 1815 peasants owned much of the land in small farms.
French farms stayed small and methods were slow to change. Many peasants stayed on the land, which slowed migration into industry.
In Prussia the Stein–Hardenberg reforms began with the October Edict of 1807 (Stein), which abolished hereditary serfdom (peasants bound to the land and owing service to a lord), in effect from 1810.
Hardenberg's Regulation Edict of 1811 let peasants become owners of their land, but only by surrendering part of it, often a third to a half, to the lord. This is why the nobility kept large estates.
The Junker estates (the big estates of the Prussian landowning nobility) of the east grew large and were modernised. They produced grain for export and for the growing cities.
New crops spread on the continent: the potato became the staple (main everyday food) of the poor, and sugar beet was grown in France and the German lands.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Stein (1807 edict) and Hardenberg (1811 edict). Naming both, with what each did, is the kind of dated evidence essays are rewarded for.

notes.h: The hungry 1840s and emigration
notes.b: The poor depended on a few crops, so when those failed the result was hunger across much of Europe. The crisis also pushed people to leave.
points: The potato blight (a disease that rots the crop) struck from 1845, and grain harvests were poor in 1846 and 1847. Food prices rose and there was hunger and food riots across western and central Europe.
In Britain the 1840s are often called the 'Hungry Forties'.
The hunger came together with a commercial and industrial depression in 1847, which helped create the conditions for the revolutions of 1848.
Emigration from the German lands to the United States grew strongly in the late 1840s and 1850s, as rural people and artisans (skilled craft workers) sought land and work abroad.
Ireland also lost many people. In the Famine of 1845–49 about a million died and about a million emigrated.
notes.tip: Use the 1840s crisis as hunger evidence in a farm-workers essay and as a cause in the economic background to 1848. It needs only a clause in the second case.

notes.h: Industrialisation in Britain: steam and cotton
notes.b: Three industries led the first industrial revolution: coal, iron and cotton textiles, with the factory and steam power at the centre. Steam and cotton show how invention changed where and how people worked.
points: James Watt improved the steam engine, patenting a separate condenser in 1769 and adding rotary motion (turning a wheel) from the 1780s. His partner was Matthew Boulton of Birmingham.
Steam was used to pump water out of coal mines and to drive machinery in factories. Because engines did not need a river, factories no longer had to be built beside fast water.
Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769) and Samuel Crompton's spinning mule (1779) mechanised spinning, the making of thread from fibre.
Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785) spread weaving into factories as well. Hand-loom weavers, who worked at home, declined as a result.
Raw cotton for the Lancashire mills was imported in large quantities, mostly from the southern United States.
Britain became the leading exporter of cotton goods, which is why Lancashire was the centre of the industry.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level paragraphs score best with short, dated facts: Watt, Arkwright's water frame (1769), Crompton's mule (1779), Lancashire cotton.

notes.h: Iron, steel and the workshop of the world
notes.b: Machines, rails and bridges all needed iron, and later steel. Britain's lead in metals showed in 1851, when it put its industry on show.
points: Abraham Darby's coke smelting at Coalbrookdale in Shropshire (1709) used coke (coal heated to remove impurities) to smelt iron. It was background to the growth of the iron industry, which produced iron on a larger scale.
Iron was used for rails, bridges and machines, which is why iron and coal grew together with railways and factories.
Henry Bessemer's converter (1856) made steel cheaply. Steel is stronger than iron, and cheap steel was the basis of later heavy industry.
The Great Exhibition of 1851 was held in the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, London. It showed Britain as the 'workshop of the world', a nickname for the leading industrial nation.
notes.tip: Mention Bessemer and 1856 when writing about steel in a Higher essay on changes in industry.

notes.h: Railways in Britain and their effects
notes.b: Railways combined iron, coal and steam. They changed how goods and people moved and created demand for more industry.
points: The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825, so steam locomotives were already in use before the Liverpool line.
The Stephensons' Rocket (built by George and Robert Stephenson) won the Rainhill Trials in 1829, showing that steam locomotives could haul trains effectively.
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened on 15 September 1830. It was the first inter-city railway worked by steam locomotives, with timetabled passenger trains.
A railway boom, known as 'railway mania', followed in Britain in the mid-1840s, and the rail network expanded rapidly.
Railways made transport of goods and people cheaper and faster, and they created national markets instead of local ones.
They created demand for coal, iron and engineering, and they gave work in construction, so railways pulled other industries along.
notes.tip: Keep Stockton and Darlington (1825) and Liverpool and Manchester (1830) apart, and name Rocket as the Stephensons' engine, not George's alone.

notes.h: Why the continent was slower, and Belgium first
notes.b: Britain's lead did not mean the rest of Europe followed at once. Obstacles delayed continental industry, but Belgium overcame them first.
points: The continent was slower because of the French wars, poorer transport, internal tariffs (taxes on goods crossing borders) and many separate states in the German lands, less accessible coal and smaller markets.
A peasantry that stayed on the land also meant fewer workers moved into factories.
Continental states copied British machines and hired British engineers to catch up.
Belgium was the first country on the continent to industrialise, with coal in Hainaut and Liège. It had the advantage of coal, which powered engines and furnaces.
John Cockerill, who was English-born, set up ironworks and engineering works at Seraing, near Liège, in 1817.
The Brussels–Mechelen railway, opened on 5 May 1835, was Belgium's first railway, steam-worked and the first stage of a state-built network.

Continental industry relied more on investment banks and on state help, through railways and tariffs, than British industry did. In Britain firms grew largely from their own profits and private capital.
notes.tip: Say 'Belgium's first railway', not first on the continent. The Saint-Étienne–Andrézieux line of 1827 was earlier, though horse-drawn at first.

notes.h: Industrialisation in France
notes.b: France industrialised more slowly than Britain or Belgium. Its growth was mixed, with some regions advanced and a large rural population behind.
points: Textile industry developed in Alsace (Mulhouse) and Normandy (Rouen), such as cotton spinning and weaving.
The Schneider brothers took over the ironworks at Le Creusot in 1836, for example, building up iron and engineering in central France.
The Saint-Étienne–Andrézieux line of 1827 carried coal and was horse-drawn at first.
The Railway Law of 11 June 1842 set out a national network in which the state provided the land and track bed while private companies laid the track and ran the lines.
Growth was faster in the 1850s and 1860s under the Second Empire.
notes.tip: A Higher essay needs 'how fast in each country'. For France, name the French law of 1842 and explain the slower pace by small peasant farms.

notes.h: Industrialisation in the German lands
notes.b: The German lands industrialised late but fast. Removing barriers between states and building on rich coalfields let them catch up.
points: The Zollverein (customs union) of 1834 removed internal tariffs between member states, so trade and investment grew across the German lands.
The first German railway ran from Nuremberg to Fürth in Bavaria and opened on 7 December 1835.
The Ruhr and Silesian coalfields grew rapidly, which gave cheap fuel for iron and steel.
Alfred Krupp's works at Essen expanded from the 1850s, and the steel industry of the Ruhr was built on coal and iron from the region.
Friedrich List argued in The National System of Political Economy (1841) for railways and protective tariffs for young German industry.
By 1871 Germany was becoming the leading industrial power on the continent.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Nuremberg–Fürth (December 1835, Germany's first) with Brussels–Mechelen (May 1835, Belgium's first). Friedrich List is the economist, not Liszt the composer.

notes.h: The factory system and working conditions
notes.b: The factory changed how people lived their working lives. Instead of working at home at their own pace, workers had to obey the machine and the clock.
points: The factory system concentrated workers under supervision, working fixed hours to the pace of the machines for wages, with fines and discipline for lateness or mistakes.
Hand workers such as handloom weavers declined because machines produced cloth more cheaply.
Hours were long, often 12 to 14 a day in cotton mills, so workers had little time or energy outside work.
Children and women made up a large share of the textile workforce, and children could start work at an early age because they were cheap to employ.
Unfenced machinery caused accidents and injuries, and little or no compensation was paid to injured workers.
Poor ventilation, dust and heat made mills unhealthy, so lung disease and exhaustion were common.
In the mines, children and women worked underground in dangerous conditions, such as hauling coal in the dark.
notes.tip: Industrial workers in a Higher essay: hours, child labour, accidents, slums and cholera, and the workhouse. Name the reforms and their limits.

notes.h: Protest, inquiry and the factory laws
notes.b: Workers resisted the machines, reformers gathered evidence, and Parliament passed laws. Each law covered a particular group and place, so you need to know which is which.
points: The Luddites (1811–16, in the Midlands and the North of England) broke machines, which showed the hostility of hand workers who feared losing their living.
The Sadler Committee of 1832 (led by Michael Sadler MP) gathered evidence of the abuse of child workers. Lord Ashley, later 7th Earl of Shaftesbury, campaigned for factory reform.
The Factory Act of 1833 barred children under nine from textile mills (silk mills excepted), and limited children of 9–13 to nine hours and young persons of 13–18 to twelve hours a day.
The 1833 Act also required two hours' schooling a day for child workers, and four inspectors were appointed to enforce it.
The Mines Act of 1842 banned women and girls, and boys under ten, from working underground.
The Ten Hours Act of 1847 limited women and young persons in textile mills to ten hours a day. A Factory Act of 1844 came in between.
notes.tip: Distinguish the Factory Act 1833 (children in textile mills, inspectors), the Mines Act 1842 (underground work) and the Ten Hours Act 1847 (women and young persons).

notes.h: Laissez-faire and the role of the state
notes.b: Many British thinkers and governments believed the state should leave the economy alone. This belief explains both why change was so fast and why the response to its harms was slow.
points: Laissez-faire is the belief that the state should leave the economy, prices, wages and trade to the free market.

Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) argued that free trade and competition produce prosperity. Thomas Malthus (Essay on the Principle of Population, 1798) and David Ricardo (Principles of Political Economy, 1817) were later economists in this tradition.
In practice laissez-faire meant free trade, shown by the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846.

The Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 gave relief to the able-bodied poor normally only inside a workhouse, where conditions were made worse than those of the poorest independent labourer. This was the principle of 'less eligibility'.
The limits: the state did intervene in child and female labour (the Factory Acts and Mines Act) and in public health, but not in men's wages or hours.
The continent was more interventionist: Prussia and France promoted railways, tariffs and banks. List argued that young German industry needed protection.
notes.tip: Explain causes of harsh conditions with laissez-faire. Mention the workhouse with the word 'able-bodied'.

notes.h: Urban growth and migration
notes.b: Industry and farming change drew people into towns. Cities grew faster than anyone could house them, which is the root of the slum and disease problems of the industrial towns.
points: Manchester, nicknamed 'Cottonopolis', grew from about 75,000 people in 1801 to about 300,000 in 1851.
Liverpool, Leeds, Birmingham and Glasgow also grew quickly, because they were centres of trade and industry that offered work.
Migration from the countryside had push causes (enclosure, mechanisation, rural poverty and the 1840s crisis) and pull causes (factory work and wages).
Irish migrants came to British cities in large numbers, especially in the 1840s, because the Famine drove them from home.
Paris grew mainly by migration from the provinces, from about 550,000 in 1801 to about a million by the mid-1840s, with overcrowding in the old centre.

In the Ruhr, Essen, Bochum and Dortmund grew fast in the 1850s and 1860s, drawing workers from rural Prussia. Mass Polish-speaking migration came later, mainly after 1871, so it falls outside this period.
The 1851 census showed that, for the first time, more than half the population of England and Wales lived in towns.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level paragraphs on urban growth score from short facts: Manchester's two figures, other cities, Irish migrants, Paris, the 1851 census. Say England and Wales for the census.

notes.h: Slums and cholera
notes.b: Towns had grown far faster than their housing and water. The result was disease, as the poor lived in places with no drains.
points: Slums had back-to-back houses (built in rows sharing walls, with no back door or through air), cellar dwellings, overcrowding, no drains, shared privies, polluted water and smoke. Death rates were high, especially among infants.
Little Ireland in Manchester was an Irish slum by the River Medlock, described by Engels.
Friedrich Engels, in The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845, published in German), described Manchester, a witness account that influenced the debate on reform.
Cholera, a disease spread by dirty water, struck Britain in 1831–32, 1848–49 and 1853–54, and Paris in 1832 and 1849. Thousands died in each epidemic. Typhus and tuberculosis also killed.
notes.tip: Do not say thousands died in a city for Britain, which is a country. Keep Engels (Manchester, 1845) separate from Chadwick and Snow.

notes.h: Public health reform and housing
notes.b: Inquiry came first and law followed, but reform was slow because many believed the state should not interfere.
points: Edwin Chadwick's Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population of Great Britain (1842) linked dirt and poor drainage to disease and early death.
The Public Health Act of 1848 created a General Board of Health (Chadwick a member) and local boards of health.
It was largely permissive, meaning towns were not forced to act. Local boards were compulsory only where the death rate was very high.
In 1854 the London physician John Snow traced the Broad Street (Soho) cholera outbreak to a contaminated pump, showing that cholera spread through water.
After the 'Great Stink' of summer 1858, Joseph Bazalgette built London's main drainage system (sewers) from 1859.
The Peabody Trust (1862), founded by the American banker George Peabody, built model dwellings for London's poor.
The Public Health Act of 1875 made sanitary provision compulsory for local authorities, after the period.
notes.tip: Keep the Public Health Act 1848 (permissive) apart from 1875 (compulsory). Say what each of Engels, Chadwick and Snow did.

notes.h: Primary education: why states acted, Prussia and France
notes.b: As economies and states changed, governments wanted schooled populations. Prussia led, and France followed with a law of its own.
points: States expanded schooling to produce disciplined, literate workers and soldiers, and loyal citizens and subjects. Churches also had religious and moral aims.
Fear of disorder pushed states too, because schools taught obedience, and later came the need for voters who could read.

Prussia had compulsory schooling from the eighteenth century, confirmed by Frederick the Great's General School Regulations of 1763. The state supervised village schools and teachers, and teacher-training seminaries followed in the nineteenth century.
Prussia was seen as Europe's model because it had among the highest literacy rates.
The Guizot Law of 28 June 1833 (François Guizot, Minister of Public Instruction) required each commune (the smallest local government unit) to maintain a primary school, in practice for boys.
It also required each department to have a teacher-training college (école normale). Schooling was not free or compulsory for all, with free places for the poor only.
Victor Duruy's law of 1867 required communes of 500 or more inhabitants to provide a girls' school.
notes.tip: Do not say Prussia's 1763 decree was the first such law. For the Guizot Law give the commune school and the teacher-training college, and note it was not free or compulsory for all.

notes.h: Primary education in Britain before and after 1870
notes.b: Britain left schooling to churches for a long time, and the state slowly came in with money, inspection and, in 1870, its own schools.
points: Schools were run by voluntary religious societies: the Anglican National Society (1811) and the Nonconformist British and Foreign School Society (1814).
They used the monitorial system of Andrew Bell and Joseph Lancaster, in which older pupils (monitors) taught younger ones, so one teacher could manage a large class cheaply.
The first government grant for education came in 1833: £20,000, given to the two societies.

The Committee of the Privy Council on Education (1839) was set up to supervise a larger grant, raised to £30,000, with James Kay (later Kay-Shuttleworth) as secretary. School inspectors began in 1839.
The Newcastle Commission, appointed in 1858 and reporting in 1861, found many children were poorly taught.
Robert Lowe's Revised Code of 1862 introduced 'payment by results', so grants depended on pupils' results in reading, writing and arithmetic.

The Elementary Education Act of 1870, introduced by W. E. Forster, set up elected school boards to build board schools where voluntary schools were insufficient. Fees were still charged and boards could make attendance compulsory locally; national compulsion came in 1880.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level document questions expect the two societies, the grant and the Privy Council committee, the Newcastle finding and Lowe's payment by results. Do not mix up the Commission with the Revised Code.

notes.h: Rising literacy and its effects
notes.b: Schooling raised literacy, the ability to read and write, and literacy changed politics.
points: Historians measure literacy by the ability to sign the marriage register. It was highest in Prussia, Scandinavia and Scotland, lower in England and France, and much lower in southern and eastern Europe.
Literacy was higher in Protestant northern Europe and lower in the south and east, so the gap was wide across the continent.
More people could read newspapers, books and pamphlets, and a cheap popular press grew.
Political ideas, nationalism and mass politics spread, because ideas could now reach the middle and working classes in print.
notes.tip: Explain why literacy mattered: newspapers, books and the spread of nationalism.

notes.h: Assessment: gains and costs of change
notes.b: Examiners reward judgement. Weigh what the period gained against what it cost, and note that change was uneven.
points: Gains: rising output and national wealth, and more food from improved farming.
Costs: loss of land and common rights, child labour and dangerous work, slums and epidemics, and the 1840s hunger.
Gains: railways and cheaper goods, and by the end of the period reform of factories, public health and education.
Costs: government response was slow and uneven because of laissez-faire, so harm continued even after reform began.

Uneven change: Britain went first and furthest and Belgium early, France was slower with its peasant farms, and the German lands grew rapidly after 1850. Eastern and southern Europe were largely agricultural in 1871.
Contemporary views: critics at the time such as Engels, Chadwick and the factory reformers saw misery. Supporters saw progress, as at the Great Exhibition.
Later views: historians still debate whether workers' living standards rose or fell in the early decades (the 'standard of living debate'), with broad agreement that they rose after about 1850.
Verdict: real gains in wealth and education came at a heavy social cost.
notes.tip: Use paired points with evidence and finish with a verdict: gains versus costs, how far governments responded, and Britain versus the continent.

keyTerms.definition: The consolidation of open fields and common land into individually owned farms, carried out mainly by Acts of Parliament in Britain.
The shift from hand production and rural work to factory production powered by steam and based on coal, iron and machinery.
The doctrine that markets should be free from government control, which shaped British economic policy in the early nineteenth century.
The organisation of production in large workplaces where workers were supervised and worked fixed hours for wages.
The growth of towns and cities as people moved from the countryside to find work in industry.
An infectious disease spread through contaminated water, which caused repeated epidemics in European cities in the 1830s and 1840s.
The French law of 1833 that required each commune to maintain a boys' primary school and provided for teacher training.
The ability to read and write, which rose in the nineteenth century through primary education and spread political and national ideas.
The British tariffs on imported grain, introduced in 1815 to protect landowners, which Peel repealed in 1846 as a victory for free trade.

factCards.definition: The crop rotation of wheat, turnips, barley and clover, which kept land fertile and fed livestock through winter.
The Prussian reforms from 1807 that abolished personal serfdom in stages and later let peasants become owners, though many had to give up part of their land to the nobles.
James Watt improved the steam engine in the 1760s and 1770s, and steam was then applied to pumping mines and powering factories.
Richard Arkwright's water frame and Samuel Crompton's spinning mule transformed cotton spinning in Britain.
The railway opened in 1830 was the first steam-hauled passenger railway that ran to a timetable.
George Stephenson's locomotive Rocket won the Rainhill Trials in 1829, showing that steam locomotives could haul trains effectively.
Belgium was the first country on the European continent to industrialise, with coal mines in Hainaut and Liège and early iron and textile works.
The first German railway, between Nuremberg and Fürth, opened in 1835.
The British law that barred children under nine from most textile factories and limited the hours of older children, with inspectors to enforce it.
The British law that banned women and children under ten from working underground in coal mines.
The British law that required the poor to enter workhouses to receive relief, reflecting laissez-faire ideas about welfare.
Edwin Chadwick's report on the sanitary condition of the labouring population, which showed the link between poor living conditions and disease.
The London physician John Snow traced a cholera outbreak in Soho to a contaminated water pump on Broad Street in 1854.
The British law that set up school boards to provide schools where voluntary provision was inadequate.
